title: Build-failing validation and a safe refresh path for .secrets.baseline
objective: Replace prose guidance about the Windows path-separator trap with a check that FAILS THE BUILD. .secrets.baseline has been corrupted four times by four different code paths, twice after the failure was documented at HIGH confidence and read by the person who then hit it. Add a validator that pins DIRECTION (posix keys always, counts non-decreasing, tracked files never disappearing, hashes well-formed), a refresh path that normalises to posix before writing so a Windows refresh updates rather than wipes, and correct exit-code handling at every invocation route.
measured_premise: P1 MEASURED 2026-08-14 on base 7577b619: the committed .secrets.baseline holds exactly 21 tracked files, 75 total entries, 0 backslash keys, 0 absolute keys, and every hashed_secret is 40-hex. The owner-supplied premise is CONFIRMED exactly.

P2 MEASURED from installed detect-secrets 1.5.0 source: detect_secrets.util.path.convert_local_os_path converts '/' to os.sep on load_from_baseline AND on scan_file, but SecretsCollection.json() serialises the internal keys with NO reverse conversion. The asymmetry is one-way, so every write path on Windows emits backslash keys. This is the generalised root cause.

P3 MEASURED from source: detect_secrets.pre_commit_hook.main returns 0 clean, 1 findings, and 3 after it has REWRITTEN the baseline via baseline.save_to_file. Exit 3 means the file changed on disk, not that a secret was found.

P4 POSITIVE CONTROL MEASURED: detect-secrets-hook --baseline .secrets.baseline over all tracked files on Windows exits 0 and leaves the blob byte-identical at e729444e8c164abce60bb9bc8153bfbbfa2ba19f. The hook is quiet when nothing needs updating, which is why routine scripts/check.ps1 runs pass and corruption only appears during real work.

P5 MEASURED (failure mode B, real route): shifting line numbers in one fixture makes detect-secrets-hook exit 3 and rewrite ALL 21 file keys with backslashes while preserving all 75 entries. Entry counts are UNCHANGED, so a count-direction guard is structurally blind to mode B.

P6 MEASURED (failure mode B, second route): detect-secrets scan --baseline .secrets.baseline rewrites the file IN PLACE, exits 0 SILENTLY, produces the same 21 backslash keys, and additionally injects a 13th filter (is_baseline_file) that the committed baseline does not carry.

P7 MEASURED: neither stock route DELETED an entry; both preserved all 75. Failure mode A (deletion) is therefore attributable to bespoke posix-keyed merge logic layered over native-keyed scan output, not to detect-secrets alone. The owner brief's framing is corrected accordingly.
in_scope: scripts/check_secrets_baseline.py (new; stdlib-only structural and directional validator)
scripts/refresh_secrets_baseline.py (new; posix-normalising safe refresh wrapper with correct exit-code handling)
tests/unit/test_secrets_baseline.py (new; structural invariants plus permanent reproductions of failure modes A and B and the legitimate-refresh false-positive control)
.pre-commit-config.yaml (add a local validator hook AFTER the detect-secrets hook so an auto-rewrite fails the commit)
.github/workflows/ci.yml (run the validator in the secrets job; make exit-code handling explicit)
scripts/check.ps1 and scripts/check.sh (run the validator; distinguish exit 0 / 1 / 3)
CONTRIBUTING.md (document the safe refresh procedure and the exit codes)
out_of_scope_zero_diff: .secrets.baseline ITSELF. It must stay byte-identical at blob e729444e8c164abce60bb9bc8153bfbbfa2ba19f. If the validator proves the committed file already invalid, STOP and report rather than silently repairing it.
agent-state/feature_list.json (byte-identical to base; F008 stays passes:false)
any manifest, lockfile, override, or audit configuration (the nanoid GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8 Dependency audit failure is an accepted, documented risk that also fails on untouched main)
promotion or merge of the draft pull request
acceptance_criteria: A1 POSITIVE CONTROL: the validator PASSES on the committed baseline at base. A failure it reports later therefore means something.

A2 FAILURE MODE B: a baseline whose result keys contain backslashes FAILS the validator, naming the offending keys. Proved against the artefact produced by the real detect-secrets-hook rewrite, not a hand-typed imitation.

A3 FAILURE MODE A: a baseline with a tracked file removed entirely, and a baseline with one file's entry count reduced, both FAIL the validator. Direction is pinned, not merely scope: a deletion is a change, and the check must reject it BECAUSE it is a deletion.

A4 NO FALSE POSITIVE: a legitimate refresh that updates a digest and a line number IN PLACE, preserving every file and every per-file count, PASSES. A false positive here would teach people to bypass the check, which is worse than no check.
A5 NO FALSE POSITIVE ON GROWTH: adding a new file entry, or new entries to an existing file, PASSES. The check is non-decreasing, not equality.
A6: a hashed_secret that is not 40-hex lowercase FAILS.
A7: the validator fails on a stale entry naming a file that no longer exists in the working tree.

A8: the refresh wrapper produces posix keys from a Windows run, preserves every pre-existing file entry, refuses to write a result that would fail validation, and reports exit 3 as 'the baseline changed' rather than as a finding.
A9: every invocation route is covered - the pre-commit hook, scripts/check.ps1, scripts/check.sh, and CI - or is explicitly shown to be safe unchanged.
A10: exit code 3 is never reported as a secret finding and never treated as silent success at any route.
A11: the diff is limited to approved files, .secrets.baseline is byte-identical to base proved by blob hash, and the pull request remains DRAFT.
verification_plan: Re-derive origin/main with git ls-remote before branching and again immediately before reporting.
State a prediction BEFORE each measurement, then record the measured outcome including where the prediction was wrong.
Reproduce failure modes A and B on a detached scratch worktree outside the repository, never on the real tree.
Run the validator as a positive control on the committed baseline before trusting any failure it reports.
Test the mode-B artefact under a real LINUX container to establish whether CI would have caught it, rather than inferring from convert_local_os_path.
Prove .secrets.baseline restoration by BLOB HASH (git hash-object vs git rev-parse ref:path), never numstat.
Run the full suite and scripts/check.ps1, and run any filtered git diff UNFILTERED first as a positive control.
Open a draft PR and inspect its state with gh pr view.
negative_tests: Backslash keys must FAIL even though the entry count is unchanged, because mode B preserves counts.
A removed file entry must FAIL even though every surviving entry is byte-identical, because a deletion is a change and the previous guard passed on exactly this.
A reduced per-file count must FAIL even when no file disappeared.
An in-place digest and line-number update must PASS, or the check will be bypassed.
An absolute path, a drive-lettered path, a './'-prefixed path, or a '..' segment must FAIL.
The validator must fail loudly rather than pass silently when it cannot resolve a reference baseline under --require-reference.
data_implications: No migration, no schema change, no persisted state. .secrets.baseline is not modified by this slice; only the machinery that guards and refreshes it is added.
security_privacy: This slice strengthens a security control. It adds no network access, no credential handling, and no dependency. The baseline's hashed_secret values are SHA-1 digests (for the fixture entries, digests of SHA-256 digests) and never credential material; the validator only checks their SHAPE and never their content.
portability: Standard library only; no new dependency. The validator runs identically on Windows and Linux and is deliberately platform-agnostic, since the defect it guards is a platform asymmetry.
z0_risk: Indirect but real. A corrupted secrets baseline degrades the control that keeps credential material out of a public repository whose entire product claim depends on published evidence being trustworthy. A silently wiped baseline turns a passing secret scan into a vacuous one.
